summary:
IGNIS-PSI, an interactive web workbench designed to help engineers and researchers make sense of NASA’s microgravity fire safety data. Because flames behave completely differently without gravity, valuable findings across NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database are often scattered and hard to compare. Our platform brings together 19 real NASA studies and 140 published papers into one clean, searchable workspace.

Users can rank and compare experiments side by side, simulate fire risks inside future Lunar and Martian habitats with higher oxygen levels and low airflow, and explore how microgravity smoke detection and suppression systems work. We also built a Mission Safety Audit powered by real machine-learning models trained directly on the NASA dataset to forecast future fire hazards and highlight where partial gravity flight data is still missing. Ultimately, IGNIS-PSI turns complex orbital research into clear safety decisions for astronauts and translates those same insights to protect firefighters and electric-vehicle systems here on Earth.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

IGNIS-PSI is an interactive scientific research and fire-safety intelligence workbench built around NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database for the "Flame in Freefall" challenge. It ingests 19 real NASA investigations—13 official PSI ISA-Tab datasets (PSI-20 through PSI-159) and 6 NASA technical PDF studies—into 78 context-injected chunks and 140 peer-reviewed DOIs, each tagged with physical parameters (oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow speed, gravity regime, hardware rack, fuel phase, and safety pillar). On top of this corpus, it provides five connected modules: (1) a Hybrid PSI Ranker and Side-by-Side Comparison Matrix to inspect experimental objectives, fuel geometries, within-study variables, sensors, and hardware facilities (CIR, MDCA, ACME, MSG, SoFIE, SAFFIRE); (2) a Habitat Flammability Modeler simulating ISS (21% O2, 14.7 psia), Lunar Exploration Atmospheres (34% O2, 8.2 psia), EVA suits (100% O2, 4.3 psia), the BASS-II Goldilocks low-velocity airflow hazard (0–40 cm/s), and 0g–1g partial-gravity bounds; (3) a Detection and Suppression analyzer comparing SAME 0.2 µm ultrafine smoke thresholds against legacy 1.0 µm ISS alarms, DAFT dust crossover, ACME CFI-G cool-flame reignition, and FLEX/water-mist extinguishment; (4) a Mission Safety Audit powered by non-mocked Scikit-Learn models (a 120-tree RandomForestClassifier with k-NN matching and a TF-IDF + LogisticRegression NLP anomaly classifier achieving 86% 5-fold cross-validation accuracy) trained directly on the 19 NASA studies; and (5) an Earth Spin-Offs and Ask SI Engineer module with DOI-cited answers.

What benefits does it have?

Instead of forcing engineers, researchers, and students to manually sift through dozens of disconnected ISA-Tab spreadsheets and dense PDFs, IGNIS-PSI turns NASA’s combustion archive into immediate, verifiable engineering decisions. Users can compare experiments side by side, test habitat atmospheres dynamically with live pO2 and kPa telemetry, export Markdown safety briefs in one click, and run real-time hazard classifications without any mocked data.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Its primary intended impact is making future Artemis Lunar habitats, pressurized rovers, and Mars transit spacecraft safer by preventing mission designers from relying blindly on Earth (1g) or ISS (0g) flammability assumptions. At the same time, it accelerates terrestrial fire-safety spin-offs by connecting orbital research—such as fine water-mist extinguishers, 0.2 µm ultrafine aerosol sensing, and composite flammability limits—to EV battery thermal-runaway detection, firefighter protective gear, and confined-space air safety on Earth.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We built the backend in Python 3 using FastAPI (0.163.1), Pydantic (2.14.3), Uvicorn, Scikit-Learn (1.9.1 RandomForestClassifier, TfidfVectorizer, LogisticRegression, StandardScaler, NearestNeighbors, StratifiedKFold), NumPy (2.5.5), and Python unittest. The frontend was built with React (18.3.1), Vite (6.0.5), Tailwind CSS (v4.0.0), Recharts (2.15.0), and Lucide React (0.468.0), featuring a Cmd+K Command Palette and Obsidian Dark / Studio Light themes. Data ingestion and version control used custom PSI ISA-Tab/PDF parsers and GitHub.

How is your project creative?

Most dashboards summarize existing studies and stop there. IGNIS-PSI’s core creative insight is auditing what NASA still does not know: our Empirical Coverage & Gap Matrix explicitly flags regimes with zero direct flight data such as solid flammability in 1/6g Lunar and 3/8g Martian gravity pending upcoming LUCI and FM2 missions—and pairs that gap analysis with real, non-mocked machine-learning forecasts trained strictly on the NASA corpus rather than synthetic datapoints.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team accounted for non-intuitive microgravity physics (absence of buoyancy, upstream Goldilocks flame spread at 5–15 cm/s, reduced nitrogen thermal ballast in 34% O2 atmospheres, invisible cool-flame reignition, and 0.2 µm sub-micron smoke aerosols), strict scientific provenance (every metric and answer traces back to exact PSI study IDs and DOIs with SI/Imperial psia, kPa, and pO2 units), and multi-audience usability through switchable Engineer, Researcher, and Student lenses.
